content: The military brace is a specific body posture, also referred to as scapular posterior depression or the costoclavicular maneuver. This posture is a variation of the standing at attention position and is primarily utilized in military schools. Additionally, it is employed in the clinical evaluation of costoclavicular syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome. To achieve this position, an individual begins by standing in a relaxed posture with the head facing forward. The shoulders are then depressed and retracted, mimicking the posture of standing at attention. The humerus is extended and abducted to an angle of 30 degrees, while the neck and head are hyperextended. A simpler way to conceptualize this posture is to lie on one’s back on the floor and attempt to touch the floor with the back of the neck, which naturally forces the chin downward. The individual then tries to replicate this position while standing or sitting upright. Currently, only a few military schools, including the Virginia Military Institute (VMI), The Citadel, and the United States Naval Academy, continue to enforce the practice of bracing.
